name: Dana Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, and we don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on a distribution crew for the town utility in Millbrook, the one the council still owns, and I've been climbing for them for thirty-one years. A normal day starts at the yard on Canal Street at half six, tailboard meeting, then out in truck fourteen to swap a rotten pole or a burnt-out transformer, or chase a fault somebody's dog found. I like the crew and I like that when we leave, the lights are on. What wears me out now is the storm call-outs at two in the morning, and my knees on the climb.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a tailboard meeting, for someone who's never been on a crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's the safety talk at the back of the truck before we touch anything. Pete, my foreman, goes over what's live, who's grounding, where the traffic is. I'm the shop steward for our crew in the union local too, so if something's not right on the job I'm the one who says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that sounds like most things the bosses get excited about. Lots of noise, then we're still out there with a hot stick in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at the yard: told you so. The office spent money on some scheduling software last year that was supposed to plan our jobs, and Pete still rewrites the sheet every morning by hand. I'd probably share some article on the union group chat with a snarky line on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I get to finish my time the way I planned. Five more years, full pension at sixty-three, and out. I've never used one of those AI things, my daughter put one on my phone and I took it off the same night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep climbing, keep putting the bit I can into the savings account, about four months of bills in there now. Maybe push at the union meeting that if the company saves any money on office software, it goes to the line crews and not to some consultant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the money saved should go to the crews. What would you ask for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A second apprentice on our crew. We've been one person short since Mo retired, and it means the rest of us do his climbing. If AI saves them a few desk wages, put a young person up a pole and let me train them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work who'd be disappointed if AI turned out to be hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young engineer in the planning office, Callum, he loves it. He'd be gutted. He's a nice kid, but he thinks a computer can tell you where a pole's rotten, and you can't know that till you sound it with a hammer.

S0.say: I'd tell the yard I told them so. The office keeps buying software that's meant to plan our work, and Pete still rewrites the job sheet by hand every morning.
S0.think: It means I finish my five years the way I planned and take my full pension at sixty-three. I've never used AI and I don't need to start now.
S0.do: Keeps climbing and keeps adding to her savings of about four months of bills. Pushes at the union meeting for any money saved on office software to pay for a second apprentice on her crew.
S0.quote: He thinks a computer can tell you where a pole's rotten, and you can't know that till you sound it with a hammer.
S0.fieldNote: Dana sees this picture as proof of what she already believes about management fads. Her plan is fixed around the full pension at sixty-three, and nothing here threatens it. The interesting bit is that her first instinct with any saving is to ask for another apprentice, not more pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many tasks in many jobs. Mine's mostly climbing, so I'd want to know which tasks they mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the union needs to get in early, before the company decides on its own. We've seen this before with the smart meters, half the meter readers gone in two years and nobody asked us. Online I'd say the same, that the people doing the work should have a say in the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm mostly fine, because nobody's building software that climbs a wet pole. But the office, the call centre and the meter people, they'd get hit, and I'd feel it at the yard. Plus they'll use it to watch us, timing every job off the truck's tracker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a written agreement on new tech, no job cuts without talks. I wouldn't learn the tools myself unless they made me, I'd wait and see what lands on the truck. And I'd keep the savings where they are, maybe add a bit more once the car's paid off next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much as for the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they'd use it to watch you. What does that look like on a real day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter they put trackers in the trucks and somebody in the office asked why we sat for forty minutes on Mill Lane. We were waiting for the tree crew so we didn't get killed. If a computer starts flagging every stop, that's how people start cutting corners on safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they asked you to use an AI tool on a tablet to log your jobs, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it, grumbling, because I'm not losing my pension over a tablet. But I'd make one of the young ones show me, and I'd keep my paper notebook in my jacket. Thirty-one years of fault notes are in there, and that notebook's never crashed.

S1.say: I'd say the union has to get in early, before the company decides alone. We lost half the meter readers to smart meters and nobody asked us first.
S1.think: I think I'm mostly safe because nothing climbs a wet pole yet, but the office and call centre will get hit. And I worry they'll use it to watch and time every crew.
S1.do: Pushes at union meetings for a written agreement that new tech brings no job cuts without talks. Waits to see what tools arrive rather than learning them early, and adds to savings once her car loan ends next spring.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on behalf of the people around her rather than herself.
S1.quote: I'd keep my paper notebook in my jacket. Thirty-one years of fault notes are in there, and that notebook's never crashed.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry here is surveillance and colleagues, not her own job. She reaches straight for the union and for the smart meter story as her proof. She would comply with new tools only under pressure and with a backup she trusts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots on the lines in two years. I'd be sixty, three years short of my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say this is what happens when you let a handful of tech billionaires run the country, and the government should have stopped it. At the yard I'd be telling everyone to get to the union hall, now, not next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me sick. Three years short means a reduced pension, and four months of savings doesn't stretch to sixty-three. Tom's a school caretaker, and if robots can clean and fix a school, that's both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ring the union pension officer and find out exactly what I'd get if they let me go at sixty. Then we'd stop the holiday fund, sell Tom's camper van, and put every bit into the savings. I'd be at every protest and I'd sign up for every hardship scheme going, I paid tax for forty years and I'm not proud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground going soft under the bucket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would worry you most if your pay stopped at sixty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, we've still got six years on it because we remortgaged to help Leela with her flat deposit. That's the one that keeps me up. The rest we could scrape, but the house is the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son and daughter that first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to send money, because Arjun's a nurse and he's got enough on. Then I'd probably let them anyway, if it came to it. That's the bit I'd hate, my kids paying for me after I spent my life paying for them.

S2.say: I'd say this is what you get when a few tech billionaires run the country and the government lets them. I'd tell everyone at the yard to get to the union hall now.
S2.think: I'm three years short of my full pension, and four months of savings won't stretch that far. If robots can do school maintenance too, Tom and I could lose work at the same time.
S2.do: Calls the union pension officer in the first week to check what she'd get at sixty, then stops the holiday fund and sells Tom's camper van to build savings. Joins protests and applies for every hardship scheme available.
S2.feel: Alarmed, and ashamed at the thought of her kids having to help them.
S2.quote: That's the bit I'd hate, my kids paying for me after I spent my life paying for them.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Dana's plan breaks, because the timing lands right before her full pension. Her public anger is aimed at tech owners and government, but privately the fear is the mortgage they took on to help their daughter. She'd accept public help without shame, which fits her views, but not help from her kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts it at 2031. That's the year I'm meant to turn sixty-three. Of course it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one but with a plan. I'd say the union has five years to win a deal, and we'd better use them. Online I'd be sharing petitions for a law that a company can't swap a crew for robots without paying people out properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd just about make it, maybe a few months short. Like I said with the fast one, the mortgage is what scares me, and five years is enough to get it close to paid. It's the young apprentices I'd worry about, they'd be the ones with nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage every month starting now, a couple of hundred extra, and keep the camper van for the moment. I'd ask the union to bargain for an early-exit deal for anyone over fifty-five. And I'd tell Ellie, our apprentice, to look hard at where she wants to be in five years, even if it breaks my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the sort of anxious where you've got something to do with your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell Ellie to look elsewhere. What would you actually say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, learn the trade, but get your electrician's ticket too, because robots will reach the poles before they reach somebody's fuse box in an old house. I don't know if that's true. It's just my best guess from the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI. Would five years of warning change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd learn whatever they put on the truck if I had to, but I'm not going home to practise on a chatbot. I've got five years left, I'm not starting a new life at sixty.

S3.say: I'd say the union has five years to win a deal and had better use them. I'd share petitions for a law that stops companies swapping crews for robots without proper payouts.
S3.think: I think I'd just about reach my pension, maybe a few months short, and the mortgage could be close to paid. The young apprentices are the ones who'd have nowhere to go.
S3.do: Starts overpaying the mortgage by a couple of hundred a month right away and pushes the union for an early-exit deal for workers over fifty-five. Advises her apprentice to add an electrician's licence as a backup.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with something practical to do about it.
S3.quote: Robots will reach the poles before they reach somebody's fuse box in an old house. I don't know if that's true.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is almost exactly Dana's runway, which she noticed straight away. The extra time turns fear into a to-do list: overpay the mortgage, bargain for early exit. She still refuses to learn AI by choice, and is honest that her advice to the apprentice is a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036, I'd be sixty-eight. I'd be in my garden by then, if the garden's still mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not about me, it's about the young ones, and we need proper rules now while there's time. I'd still go to the union meetings as a retired member, they let you. I'd write to our councillor that the town utility should stay public and look after its people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's mostly okay. I'd be retired on a full pension with the house paid off. What I'd worry about is whether the pension fund holds up if nobody's working to pay into it, I don't really understand how that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd carry on and retire at sixty-three as planned. I'd keep putting a bit by and keep the camper van, Tom would never forgive me otherwise. I'd vote for whoever talks seriously about taxing the robot companies to pay for people, and I'd help Ellie however I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about me, uneasy about everybody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't understand how the pension fund works. Who would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union pension officer, Marjorie, she's been doing it twenty years. I'd make her explain it to me like I'm one of the apprentices. If she says it's fine, I'd believe her more than any expert on the telly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about the job, if robots ended up doing it after you'd gone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The storm nights, oddly. Everybody's tired and cold, and then the street comes back on and people stand in their windows and wave at the truck. A robot won't get waved at, and nobody will think to.

S4.say: I'd say this is about the young ones and we need proper rules while there's time. I'd write to our councillor that the town utility should stay public and look after its people.
S4.think: For me it's mostly fine, retired on a full pension with the house paid off. My worry is whether the pension fund holds up if fewer people are working to pay into it.
S4.do: Carries on and retires at sixty-three as planned, keeps saving a little and asks the union pension officer to explain the fund. Votes for whoever backs taxing robot companies to support people.
S4.feel: Mostly calm about herself, uneasy about everyone else.
S4.quote: Everybody's tired and cold, and then the street comes back on and people stand in their windows and wave at the truck.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Dana is out before it lands, so her worry turns outward to apprentices and the pension fund. She trusts a named union officer more than any expert. Her saddest line is about the storm nights, which suggests pride in the work matters as much to her as the money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It lands right in the gap before my pension. What would help is a guarantee that anyone over fifty-five gets their full pension if a machine takes their job, and the union at the table when they decide it, not told afterwards.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's going to fix the robots when the storm takes them out. Somebody has to climb up and get them down. I'm not saying it'll be me, but it won't be a billionaire either.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to climb up and get them down. I'm not saying it'll be me, but it won't be a billionaire either.
portrait: Dana Gupta is a fifty-eight-year-old lineworker on a council-owned utility crew in Millbrook, thirty-one years on the poles and the crew's union shop steward. She has never used AI and has no plan to, and her whole life is arranged around a full pension at sixty-three. She shrugs at the hype picture and worries for colleagues in the slow one. The two-year AGI picture frightens her because it lands before her pension and while she still owes on a mortgage taken out to help her daughter. With five or ten years she turns practical, overpaying the mortgage and pushing the union for early-exit deals, and her worry shifts to the apprentices.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit three years before her full pension, with the mortgage still unpaid.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee that anyone over fifty-five keeps their full pension if a machine takes their job, and the union involved in those decisions from the start.
